objectives: Trace the history of dentistry from Hesy-Ra in ancient Egypt through Fauchard, G.V. Black, and the discovery of fluoridation.
Identify the four principal dental tissues (enamel, dentin, pulp, cementum) and describe their roles.
Compare the FDI, Universal, and Palmer tooth-notation systems and count the deciduous and permanent dentitions.

slides.title: From Hesy-Ra to Fauchard — the birth of dentistry
slides.body:
**Dentistry** is the branch of medicine concerned with the teeth, gums, jaws, and the oral cavity. Its written history reaches back almost five thousand years. **Hesy-Ra** (also spelled Hesi-Re), an official who served under the Third-Dynasty pharaoh **Djoser** around **2600 BCE**, is the earliest person known to be identified with the teeth: an inscription on his tomb at Saqqara names him **"Wer-ibeh-senjw"**, often rendered as **"Chief of Dentists and Physicians"**, making him the first recorded dentist in history. Ancient texts such as the **Edwin Smith Papyrus** and the **Ebers Papyrus** describe diseases of the teeth and remedies for toothache, and the Sumerians of Mesopotamia blamed dental decay on a mythical **"tooth worm"** — a belief that persisted in folk medicine into the eighteenth century.

Classical authors advanced the field. The Greek physician **Hippocrates** (c. 460–370 BCE) and the Roman encyclopaedist **Aulus Cornelius Celsus** (c. 25 BCE–50 CE) wrote about extractions, gum disease, and wiring loose teeth. The Etruscans crafted gold dental bridges, and the Roman writer **Claudius Galen** documented oral anatomy. Yet for many centuries dentistry was practised mainly by **barber-surgeons** and travelling tooth-drawers, not by trained professionals.

The decisive turn toward a science came with the French surgeon **Pierre Fauchard** (1678–1761). In **1728** he published *Le Chirurgien Dentiste, ou Traité des Dents* ("The Surgeon Dentist, or Treatise on the Teeth"), a comprehensive two-volume work covering oral anatomy, restorative techniques, dentures, the use of fillings, and the connection between sugar and decay. Because this book systematised the entire discipline, Fauchard is universally honoured as the **"father of modern dentistry."** He introduced dental prostheses, championed the dental drill (an adapted bow-drill), and rejected the tooth-worm myth in favour of observation. The tooth diagram beside this text shows the crown, root, and the layered tissues — enamel, dentin, pulp, and cementum — that the remainder of this lesson examines in detail.

slides.title: G.V. Black, anesthesia, and the fluoride story
slides.body:
Three nineteenth- and twentieth-century developments turned dentistry into a rigorous clinical science: standardised operative technique, painless surgery, and the prevention of decay.

**Greene Vardiman Black** (1836–1915), known as **G.V. Black** and often called the "father of modern operative dentistry" in the United States, brought order to the chaos of fillings. Around **1900** he published a standardised **classification of carious lesions** (cavity classes I through V, later extended to VI), which is still taught today and described in a later lesson. He also studied the metallurgy of **dental amalgam**, formulating a balanced alloy of silver, tin, copper, and mercury that produced predictable, durable fillings, and he articulated the principle of **"extension for prevention."** Black served as dean of the **Northwestern University Dental School** and helped professionalise dental education.

The conquest of pain was equally transformative. On **December 11, 1844**, the dentist **Horace Wells** (1815–1848) used **nitrous oxide** ("laughing gas") for a tooth extraction in Hartford, Connecticut. Two years later, on **October 16, 1846**, his former associate **William Thomas Green Morton** (1819–1868), also a dentist, gave the first widely publicised demonstration of **diethyl ether** anesthesia at the **Massachusetts General Hospital** in Boston, in the operating theatre now called the **"Ether Dome,"** while surgeon **John Collins Warren** removed a neck tumour. This event launched the modern era of surgical anesthesia, and dentistry can claim a founding role in it.

Finally, prevention. In the early 1900s the dentist **Frederick McKay** investigated a strange mottling of teeth in Colorado Springs called **"Colorado brown stain"** (now known as dental fluorosis), and noticed that affected teeth were oddly resistant to decay. Working with researchers and later with **H. Trendley Dean** of the U.S. Public Health Service, the cause was traced to naturally high **fluoride** in the drinking water. Dean developed a **fluorosis index** and quantified the relationship between fluoride concentration and both mottling and caries reduction. This work led to the first deliberate community **water fluoridation**, begun in **Grand Rapids, Michigan, in 1945** — a landmark the CDC later named one of the ten great public-health achievements of the twentieth century.

slides.title: Tooth structure, dentition, and notation systems
slides.body:
A tooth is divided anatomically into the **crown** (the visible portion above the gum) and the **root** (anchored in the jawbone), meeting at the **cervical line** or neck. Four mineralised and soft tissues build it:

- **Enamel** — the outermost layer of the crown and the **hardest tissue in the human body**. It is roughly 96% inorganic **hydroxyapatite**, a calcium-phosphate mineral with the idealised formula $\mathrm{Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6(OH)_2}$. Enamel is acellular and cannot regenerate once formed.
- **Dentin** (British: dentine) — the bulk of the tooth beneath the enamel and cementum. It is about 70% mineral, contains microscopic **dentinal tubules**, and is produced by cells called **odontoblasts**. Dentin is living tissue and can be sensitive.
- **Pulp** — the soft core within the **pulp chamber** and **root canals**, containing nerves, blood vessels, and connective tissue. It supplies nutrition and sensation.
- **Cementum** — a thin, bone-like mineralised layer covering the root, into which the fibres of the periodontal ligament anchor.

Humans are **diphyodont** (we grow two sets of teeth) and **heterodont** (teeth of differing shapes). The **primary or deciduous dentition** ("baby teeth") comprises **20 teeth**, while the **permanent dentition** comprises **32 teeth** (including four third molars or "wisdom teeth"). Each arch of the permanent set contains incisors, canines, premolars, and molars.

Dentists record teeth using standardised **notation systems**. The **FDI World Dental Federation two-digit system** (ISO 3950) labels each tooth with a quadrant digit (1–4 for permanent, 5–8 for primary) followed by a tooth digit, so the upper-right central incisor is **"11"** (read "one-one"). The **Universal Numbering System**, common in the United States, numbers the permanent teeth **1 to 32** starting at the upper-right third molar; primary teeth are lettered **A to T**. The **Palmer notation** (also called the Zsigmondy–Palmer system, after **Adolf Zsigmondy** and **Corydon Palmer**) uses a bracket symbol indicating the quadrant together with a number 1–8 (or letters A–E for primary teeth). Mastering at least one notation system is essential before studying disease and treatment, because the chart is the dentist's coordinate map of the mouth.

question.question: Who is universally regarded as the "father of modern dentistry," and for what work?
options: Hesy-Ra, for the earliest tomb inscription naming a dentist around 2600 BCE.
Pierre Fauchard, for the 1728 treatise *Le Chirurgien Dentiste*, which systematised the discipline.
G.V. Black, for standardising cavity classification around 1900.
William Morton, for the 1846 demonstration of ether anesthesia.
question.explanation: Pierre Fauchard's 1728 *Le Chirurgien Dentiste* organised oral anatomy, restoration, prosthetics, and disease into a coherent science, earning him the title "father of modern dentistry." Hesy-Ra (option A) is the earliest recorded dentist, not the founder of the modern science. G.V. Black (option C) is the father of modern operative dentistry in the US but came later. Morton (option D) pioneered surgical anesthesia, a different milestone.

hints: Look for the author of a comprehensive treatise that organised the whole field.
The date is 1728 and the work is in French.
slides.workedSolution: Pierre Fauchard (1678–1761) published *Le Chirurgien Dentiste, ou Traité des Dents* in 1728. It covered anatomy, operative technique, prosthodontics, periodontal disease, and the role of sugar in decay, and it explicitly rejected the medieval "tooth worm" myth. By turning a trade practised by barber-surgeons into a documented clinical science, Fauchard earned the enduring title "father of modern dentistry." Hesy-Ra is merely the earliest named dentist; Black and Morton made later, narrower contributions.

question.question: A human has a full permanent dentition of 32 teeth and previously had a full primary dentition of 20 teeth. By how many teeth does the permanent dentition exceed the primary dentition? Give a whole number.
question.hint: Subtract the primary count from the permanent count: $32 - 20$.

question.question: Which dental tissue is the hardest in the human body and is composed of roughly 96% hydroxyapatite?
options: Enamel, the outer covering of the crown.
question.explanation: Enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, about 96% inorganic hydroxyapatite, and forms the outer crown surface. Dentin (option A) is softer and contains tubules. Cementum (option B) is a thin bone-like root covering. Pulp (option D) is the soft neurovascular tissue, not mineralised at all.

hints: It is the outermost layer you can see and touch.
It cannot regenerate because it is acellular.
slides.workedSolution: Enamel forms the crown's outer shell and is approximately 96% mineral by weight, mostly hydroxyapatite with the formula $\mathrm{Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6(OH)_2}$. This extreme mineral content makes it the hardest substance the body produces, but also means it is acellular and cannot heal itself once mature. Dentin, cementum, and pulp are all softer and, unlike enamel, contain living cells.

question.question: A new dental assistant is confused by three different tooth-numbering charts
question.prompt: A dental assistant joins a clinic that recently switched from the Universal Numbering System to the FDI two-digit system, but the old patient records still use Universal numbers and a visiting orthodontist writes in Palmer notation. The assistant asks you why three systems exist and how to avoid charting errors during the transition. Explain the logic of each system (FDI quadrant-plus-tooth digits, Universal 1–32, and Palmer's quadrant bracket), give the FDI and Universal labels for the upper-right permanent central incisor, and describe one practical safeguard the clinic should adopt.

question.question: The first community water fluoridation programme, motivated by the "Colorado brown stain" investigations, began in which city and year?
options: Colorado Springs, 1908, where McKay first observed the staining.
Boston, 1846, at the Massachusetts General Hospital.
Hartford, Connecticut, 1844, where Wells used nitrous oxide.
question.explanation: Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to deliberately fluoridate its public water in 1945, following the work of Frederick McKay and H. Trendley Dean linking natural fluoride to reduced decay. Colorado Springs (option A) is where the brown stain was first studied, not where fluoridation began. Boston 1846 (option B) and Hartford 1844 (option D) refer to the early demonstrations of surgical anesthesia, not fluoride.

hints: The year is in the mid-1940s, just after World War II.
slides.workedSolution: After Frederick McKay and H. Trendley Dean traced the caries-resistant but mottled "Colorado brown stain" teeth to naturally fluoridated water and quantified the dose–response relationship, the U.S. Public Health Service launched a controlled experiment by adding fluoride to the drinking water of Grand Rapids, Michigan, in 1945. The dramatic fall in childhood cavities that followed led to widespread adoption of community water fluoridation, later named by the CDC as one of the ten great public-health achievements of the twentieth century.
